The sky is blue because the air scatters blue light more than it scatters red light.

Sunlight looks white, but it’s actually a mix of all the colors of the rainbow. Each color travels as a wave. Blue light has shorter waves than red light. When sunlight passes through Earth’s atmosphere, it interacts with tiny molecules in the air. These molecules scatter shorter waves more strongly, sending blue light off in many different directions.

That’s why you see blue even when you look at a patch of sky far from the Sun. Some of the blue light that was originally headed somewhere else has been scattered toward your eyes.

But violet has even shorter waves than blue, so why isn’t the sky violet? Sunlight contains less violet than blue, and your eyes are less sensitive to violet. The mix of scattered colors ends up looking blue to us.

The same process explains red sunsets. When the Sun is low, its light takes a longer trip through the atmosphere to reach you. More of the blue light gets scattered out of that direct path, leaving mostly reds and oranges. So the blue of a midday sky and the red of a sunset come from the same trick of light.

A **browser cache** is a storage area where your browser keeps copies of things it has downloaded, such as images, fonts, and style files. Its job is to make websites load faster and use less data.

Imagine you visit a news site. On your first visit, your browser downloads the site’s logo. When you open another article, the browser may reuse the logo it already saved instead of downloading it again. That saves a trip to the website’s server.

How does the browser know whether its copy is still good? When the server sends a file, it can include instructions about how long the browser may reuse it without checking. Once that time is up, the browser can ask, “Has this file changed?” If it hasn’t, the server sends a short reply, and the browser uses its saved copy. If it has, the browser downloads the new version.

Sometimes a website looks outdated or displays incorrectly because the browser is using an old file. Clearing the cache can help by making the browser download fresh copies. The next visit may be slower, but later visits can speed up again. The cache is separate from cookies, which often help websites remember things like whether you’re signed in.

We watched your muzzle turn gray and your steps grow slower. Our walks got shorter, but you still stopped at all your favorite trees. We learned to leave a little earlier so you could take your time. There was no need to hurry.

The house is quieter now. We still look for you in your spot by the window, and sometimes, coming home, we forget for a second that you won’t be there. We miss you most in those ordinary moments. Thank you for fifteen years of making them wonderful. We were so lucky to be your family.

The phone began ringing at low tide.

Mara heard it from the lantern room, which was impossible. On a night like this, she couldn’t hear the kettle boil unless she stood beside it. But the ring was as clear as the one in her mother’s hallway, right down to the little catch between the first trill and the second.

She took her torch down to the rocks.

It was a yellow telephone with a rotary dial. Barnacles furred the receiver. Its cord ran into a pool, where a crab, offended by the light, backed under a ledge.

Mara had been keeper on Saint Jude’s for eleven years. She had found a wedding dress, a crate of lemons, and once a cow that was alive and angrier about it than she was. She knew better than to ask how a thing had got here before deciding what to do with it.

She picked up.

“Have you lit the lamp?” a boy asked.

“Of course I have.”

“Oh,” he said. “That must be the other one, then.”

Mara turned. Out beyond the reef, where there had never been anything to stand on, a second light swept the sea and caught her full in the face.

The phone was ringing in a pool the tide had left behind.

Mara heard it halfway down the lighthouse steps and stopped, one hand on the rail. Nobody called the island anymore. The supply boat came on Thursdays, and if the weather was bad, it came on Friday. Anything worth saying could wait until then.

She found the phone wedged between two rocks, its black cord trailing into a crack. It was the same cream color as the one her mother used to keep on the kitchen wall. As a child, Mara had imagined the cord ran all the way to the person speaking.

She picked up the receiver.

“Have you put the kettle on?” a man asked.

“No.”

“Good. Don’t go back inside.”

Above her, the lighthouse beam swept across the water. In its brief light she could see her kitchen window, warm and yellow. Someone moved past it carrying a cup.

“Who is this?”

The man took a breath. She heard a spoon tap the rim of a mug.

“I’m sorry,” he said. “I thought I’d caught you before you got home.”

Mara looked down. She was wearing her slippers. She couldn’t remember coming down the stairs at all.

A year ago, I became an engineering manager. I thought the hardest part would be making tougher technical decisions. It turned out to be learning when not to make the decision myself.

Three lessons I’m taking into year two:

**Give context before advice.** When people know why a deadline matters or which trade-offs are acceptable, they can make decisions I don’t need to be in the room for.

**Don’t save feedback for a formal conversation.** A specific observation shared soon after a meeting is easier to act on than a vague pattern brought up months later. That goes for praise, too.

**Leave room in the calendar.** Some of my most useful work happened in conversations I hadn’t planned: an engineer thinking through a tricky decision, or a teammate raising a concern they hadn’t found the right moment to share.

I still enjoy solving technical problems. I’m learning to take just as much satisfaction in helping someone else solve one.

My first year as an engineering manager taught me that being helpful doesn’t always mean having the answer.

Early on, I jumped into technical discussions because I thought I could save the team time. Sometimes I did. Other times, my suggestion sounded like a decision, and the conversation ended before we’d heard the best idea.

A few habits I’m taking into year two:

• Say what’s fixed and what’s open. People make better decisions when they know which constraints are real.
• Protect time for feedback. A specific observation shared this week is more useful than a polished paragraph at review time.
• Ask what I can take off someone’s plate before offering advice on how to carry it.

I still enjoy solving technical problems. But some of my best days this year were the ones when someone else solved a hard problem and told me, “I knew I had room to try.”

### *Pride and Prejudice* by Jane Austen

Elizabeth Bennet is the second of five daughters in a family whose estate will pass to a male cousin. Her mother is eager to marry the girls off, but Elizabeth would rather risk financial insecurity than marry someone she cannot respect. When the wealthy Mr. Darcy dismisses her at a local dance, she takes him for an arrogant snob. Darcy, meanwhile, grows attracted to Elizabeth despite his reservations about her family. His first proposal manages to insult her and declare his love at the same time, and she turns him down.

A letter from Darcy forces Elizabeth to reconsider her trust in the charming Mr. Wickham. Later, when Wickham runs away with Elizabeth’s youngest sister, Lydia, Darcy quietly arranges their marriage, sparing the Bennets a scandal. By the time he proposes again, Elizabeth has revised her opinion of him, and Darcy has learned to take her criticisms seriously.

Austen’s comedy asks how well people can judge one another when vanity, class, and money shape what they see. Elizabeth is right about Darcy’s initial arrogance but wrong to assume her first impression tells her everything. The novel also treats marriage as an economic decision, even as it makes mutual respect the basis of its happiest match.

### *Pride and Prejudice* by Jane Austen

Elizabeth Bennet is one of five sisters whose family estate will pass to a male cousin, making marriage a matter of financial security. When the wealthy Charles Bingley moves into the neighborhood, he falls for Elizabeth’s older sister, Jane. Elizabeth, meanwhile, takes an immediate dislike to his friend Mr. Darcy, whose reserve strikes her as arrogance. She trusts the charming George Wickham’s account of Darcy’s past and rejects Darcy’s first proposal, accusing him of mistreating Wickham and separating Jane from Bingley.

Darcy’s letter forces Elizabeth to reconsider both accusations and recognize how readily she believed a story that confirmed her opinion. Later, when her youngest sister Lydia runs away with Wickham, Darcy quietly arranges their marriage, protecting the Bennet family from scandal. Bingley returns to Jane, and Elizabeth accepts Darcy’s second proposal, having come to respect him as he has learned to temper his pride.

The novel examines how vanity and social rank distort judgment. Austen also treats marriage as an economic institution, not merely a romantic ideal: Elizabeth’s friend Charlotte Lucas marries for security, a choice the novel makes understandable without making it enviable. Elizabeth and Darcy’s eventual happiness depends on their willingness to admit error and change.

The printing press changed Europe by making written information cheaper to produce and easier to share. Before Johannes Gutenberg developed his movable-type printing system in the mid-fifteenth century, most European books were copied by hand. Printing required considerable work up front, but once the type was set, a printer could produce hundreds of copies. Books became more affordable, and pamphlets could carry new ideas from one city to another in a matter of weeks.

One striking example was the Protestant Reformation. Printers reproduced Martin Luther’s arguments and translations, reaching readers far beyond the towns where he preached. His opponents used the same presses to answer him. Religious disputes that might once have remained local became debates across Europe, harder for any single authority to contain.

Print also changed how people learned and worked. More books appeared in vernacular languages rather than Latin, giving readers access to texts in languages they already spoke. Scholars could consult the same editions, compare findings, and point out errors. Maps, diagrams, and technical manuals could circulate alongside religious and literary works.

Printing did not make everyone literate overnight, nor did it guarantee that what people read was true. Its lasting impact was to give ideas a wider audience and make them easier to preserve, challenge, and build upon.

The printing press changed Europe because it made written material much cheaper and faster to produce. Before Johannes Gutenberg developed his press in the mid fifteenth century, most European books were copied by hand. Printers could now produce hundreds of copies of the same text, making books more affordable and giving more people a reason to learn to read.

Printing also changed who could participate in public debate. Publishers issued books and pamphlets in languages such as German, French, and English, reaching readers who did not know Latin. During the Protestant Reformation, Martin Luther’s arguments spread rapidly in print. His opponents used the same technology to answer him, but religious and political authorities found it harder to contain controversies once copies circulated across borders.

The press also helped scholars build on one another’s work. Readers in different cities could consult the same diagrams, tables, and descriptions, making it easier to compare findings and spot errors. Printers still made mistakes, and false claims could travel as readily as useful discoveries. The decisive change was not that printed information was more trustworthy, but that it could reach more people, travel farther, and remain available long enough for readers to challenge it or put it to use.

I woke to rain ticking against my hotel window and decided to give up on the Golden Gate Bridge before breakfast. At the Ferry Building, I bought a coffee and a warm cardamom bun, then stood under the arcade watching a ferry ease out into the gray. By the time I reached Chinatown, my umbrella had flipped inside out twice, so I folded it and ducked into a bakery for an egg tart. The woman behind the counter handed me an extra napkin, which I assumed was for the tart until she pointed at the water dripping from my sleeves. Later, at City Lights, I bought a paperback mostly because I wanted an excuse to stay upstairs a little longer. The rain let up just before dusk, and I walked down Columbus Avenue past restaurant windows fogged by the dinner rush. At the corner, a cable car rattled by with three passengers on the open side, all of them looking considerably colder than they had probably planned. I never did see the bridge that day. But back at the hotel, I found a flake of egg tart pastry tucked into the cuff of my coat and wished I’d bought two.

Rain followed me out of the Powell Street station and up the hill, where cable cars rattled past with their windows fogged. I ducked into a narrow cafe for coffee and watched a delivery cyclist shake water from his sleeves before ordering an espresso. By the time I reached Chinatown, rainwater was spilling from the striped awnings, and the bakery on the corner had just put out warm egg tarts. I ate one under an awning, brushing flakes of pastry from my coat while shoppers stepped around puddles with bags of greens. At the Ferry Building, I bought a bowl of clam chowder and took it outside during a lull. The Bay Bridge kept disappearing behind low clouds, but I could hear the ferries before I saw them. Later, I took the bus to Ocean Beach, where the wind turned my umbrella inside out and a dog sailed past me toward the surf. I gave up on the umbrella and walked back along Judah Street, looking for somewhere to dry off. At dinner, I hung my coat on the back of a chair and ordered a second bowl of soup, mostly because I wasn't ready to put it back on.

The first sip makes a strong case for this little ramen shop. The broth is rich without being heavy, with a deep roasted flavor and just enough salt to keep you reaching for the spoon. Springy noodles hold up to the last bite, and the soft egg has the kind of jammy yolk that makes you wish you had ordered another.

The catch is the wait. On my visit, it took nearly fifteen minutes to order and another half hour for the bowl to arrive. The staff were friendly when they made it to the table, but nobody checked in or offered an update. By the time dinner landed, I had already finished my drink.

I would go back for that broth, especially on a cold evening. Just bring a friend you really like talking to, and save this place for a night when you have nowhere else to be.

The broth is reason enough to visit this little ramen shop. I ordered the tonkotsu, and the first spoonful had the deep, savory flavor I’d hoped for without the heaviness that sometimes makes me put down the spoon halfway through. The noodles stayed springy, the pork was tender, and the scallions added a welcome bite. I finished every drop.

Getting that bowl, however, took nearly forty minutes after I ordered. The dining room was busy but not full, and nobody mentioned the delay until I asked. When the server did stop by, they were friendly and apologetic. A heads up at the start would have made the wait much less frustrating.

I’d happily come back on a quiet evening, especially if I could grab a counter seat and watch the kitchen. For a quick lunch, though, I’d go elsewhere. That broth deserves your attention, but the service demands your patience.

Remote work helps junior engineers when teams teach deliberately, but it hurts them when independence becomes an excuse for neglect. In an office, a new engineer can overhear why a design changed, notice how a senior colleague investigates a bug, or ask a quick question without scheduling a meeting. Those small encounters teach lessons that rarely make it into onboarding documents. Remotely, the same engineer can spend hours stuck because asking for help feels like interrupting someone. Yet offices do not guarantee good mentorship, and remote teams can offer advantages of their own. Written design discussions let newcomers revisit decisions at their own pace, recorded demos make unfamiliar systems easier to explore, and flexible schedules can give people more time for focused practice. The difference is whether the team makes learning part of the job. A mentor who pairs regularly, explains the reasoning behind code review comments, and checks in before a blocker becomes a lost afternoon can make remote work an excellent starting point. I would choose that team over an office where everyone is too busy to teach. For junior engineers, the question is not where they sit, but how easily they can ask for help and learn from it.

Remote work helps junior engineers when their teams make mentorship a priority, but it hurts them when independence is treated as a prerequisite rather than a skill to develop. In an office, a new engineer can overhear how a senior colleague diagnoses a bug, ask a quick question without booking a meeting, or notice that someone else is struggling with the same tool. Those moments are easy to lose online. Yet remote work can make learning more accessible: written decisions give newcomers something to revisit, thoughtful code reviews explain tradeoffs, and a flexible schedule can give people more time to concentrate. The difference is whether a junior engineer knows whom to ask, feels comfortable asking, and gets an answer before losing half a day. Teams can close that gap by pairing regularly, assigning a mentor with time to help, and giving juniors small projects they can own from start to finish. Simply requiring office attendance does not guarantee any of that. I would choose a remote team with strong mentoring over an office where everyone wears headphones and guards their calendar. For junior engineers, the decisive factor is not where they sit, but how quickly they get feedback they can use.

Running and swimming both improve cardiovascular fitness and endurance, but they suit different needs. Running is easier to fit into most routines: you need little equipment, and you can head out from your front door. It mainly works the lower body, and because it’s weight-bearing, it can help maintain bone density. The repeated impact, however, can be uncomfortable for people with joint pain, especially if they increase their distance or speed too quickly.

Swimming offers a low-impact workout because the water supports your weight. Moving against water resistance works the shoulders, back, core, and legs, making swimming a more full-body activity than running. It can be a good option if running aggravates your joints. On the other hand, swimming requires access to a pool or a safe place to swim, and beginners may need to develop their stroke and breathing technique before they can swim continuously at a comfortable pace.

If convenience and bone health are priorities, running has an edge. If you want a low-impact workout that uses more of your upper body, swimming may be a better fit. The best choice is the one you enjoy enough to do regularly, and alternating between the two can give you the benefits of both.

Running and swimming both improve cardiovascular fitness and endurance. The better choice depends on what you enjoy, how your body responds, and what fits your routine.

Its repetitive impact, however, can be uncomfortable for some people, especially if they increase their mileage too quickly.

Swimming offers a workout with much less impact. The water supports your body, while its resistance challenges your shoulders, back, core, and legs. That can make swimming a good option if running bothers your joints. The trade-off is that you need access to a pool or a safe place to swim, and beginners may find that breathing and stroke technique limit their workout before their fitness does.

If convenience and bone strength matter most, running has an edge. If you prefer less impact and more upper-body work, swimming may suit you better. You can also alternate between them for variety, but the best choice is the one you can keep doing regularly.

1/5 Clever code makes you say, “Wow, how does that work?” Simple code lets you skip straight to, “Where do I make the change?” The second question comes up a lot more often.

2/5 A one-liner isn’t necessarily simpler than five lines. If those five lines name the intermediate steps, the reader can see what the code is doing without running it in their head.

3/5 Simple code makes bugs easier to pin down. When parsing, validation, and saving happen in separate steps, you can test each one—and tell which failed when something goes wrong.

4/5 Sometimes the clever solution *is* worth it. If a benchmark shows the straightforward version is too slow, optimize the bottleneck. Keep the tricky part small and leave a comment explaining why it’s there.

5/5 Before you ship, ask: “Could someone who didn’t write this safely change it?” That someone might be you in six months.

1/5 The best code lets a teammate answer two questions quickly: What does this do? Where should I change it? If they need ten minutes to decode a one-liner, it wasn't much of a shortcut.

2/5 Simple doesn't mean fewer lines. A named variable and a plain `if` can make a business rule obvious. Squeezing both into one expression saves space but makes the reader reconstruct the rule.

3/5 At 2 a.m., nobody wants to admire your abstraction. They want to know why a retry charged a customer twice. Code that makes side effects easy to spot makes incidents easier to fix.

4/5 Sometimes cleverness earns its keep. If a benchmark shows that a trick fixes a real bottleneck, use it. Keep it in one place, explain why it's there, and test the edge cases.

5/5 Before you ship, ask: Could someone who didn't write this change it safely? If not, try a better name, a plainer branch, or one less layer of indirection. Give the next reader less to figure out.

When you’ve known someone as long as I’ve known [Name], you collect enough stories to ruin a wedding toast. You also learn which ones to save for the ride home.

So I’ll tell you this instead: [Name] has always been the friend who calls the next day. Not just when something goes wrong, but when you’ve got a job interview or your dog has a vet appointment. If it matters to you, it goes on the calendar.

[Partner], one of my favorite things about watching you two together is seeing [Name] get that same kind of care in return. And I love hearing you laugh from the kitchen when neither of you can explain, by the time you come back, what was so funny.

So here’s to a long life together, full of ordinary Tuesdays, good news worth calling about, and jokes that never quite make it out of the kitchen.

Good evening, everyone. I've known Alex since we were small enough to think that staying up past nine was a wild night. Back then, Alex was the friend who saved me a seat, shared the good snacks, and told me when I had spinach in my teeth. Not much has changed, except now we can stay up until ten.

When Alex introduced me to Sam, I noticed something. Alex, who usually jumps in to tell the best part of any story, would sit back and listen whenever Sam told one. And Sam always looked over at Alex right before the punch line. Watching them, I got to see my oldest friend fall in love.

So please raise your glasses. To Alex and Sam: may you always save each other a seat, share the good snacks, and laugh so hard you forget whose turn it is to do the dishes. Cheers!
